nodes.label: Alexander in Anatolia
nodes.full: After the Granicus, Alexander took Sardis, Ephesus, Miletus and Halicarnassus, freed the Greek cities from Persian tributes, and marched through Lycia and Pamphylia to Gordion and the Cilician Gates, where he defeated Darius at Issus in November 333. He left satraps in place, mostly Macedonians such as Calas at Daskyleion and Antigonus in Phrygia.
nodes.src: Arrian, Anabasis 1.11–2.12; Diodorus 17.17–35; Plutarch, Alexander 17–20.

nodes.label: Halicarnassus
nodes.full: Memnon of Rhodes and the satrap Orontobates held Halicarnassus against Alexander with Greek mercenaries and the Persian fleet, until Alexander, after a hard siege, took the city and left only the citadels. The one big siege of his campaign in Anatolia, it was the last Persian stand on the coast.
nodes.src: Arrian, Anabasis 1.20–23; Diodorus 17.23–27.

nodes.label: Cities freed
nodes.full: Alexander, at Ephesus and in the other cities, overthrew the oligarchies put in by the Persians, restored democracies and set aside the tribute they had paid to the king. He asked for contributions for the war instead. The cities of Anatolia became, in theory, allies of Macedon.
nodes.src: Arrian, Anabasis 1.17–18.

nodes.label: Carve-up of the empire
nodes.full: Anatolia, in the middle of the Successors' lands, was fought over by Antigonus, Lysimachus, Seleucus and Ptolemy for four decades. Its satrapies became the rooms of four rival kingdoms, then of many smaller ones.
nodes.src: Diodorus 18–20; Appian, Syrian Wars 52–63.

nodes.label: Antigonus
nodes.full: Satrap of Phrygia under Alexander, Antigonus held Anatolia against Perdiccas and Eumenes, took the royal title in 306 BC and from his capital at Antigoneia in Syria and from Celaenae tried to reunite Alexander's empire. His Anatolian base held out until the coalition defeated and killed him at Ipsus.
nodes.src: Diodorus 18–20; Plutarch, Demetrius 17–29; Arrian, Successors.

nodes.label: Ipsus
nodes.full: The armies of Antigonus and his son Demetrius met those of Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander in Phrygia. Seleucus's elephants cut Demetrius's cavalry from the infantry, Antigonus was killed, and Alexander's empire was divided among four kings for good.
nodes.src: Plutarch, Demetrius 28–29; Diodorus 20.107–113.

nodes.label: Lysimachus
nodes.full: Lysimachus, who had Thrace, took western Anatolia after Ipsus and ruled it for twenty years from Lysimacheia, rebuilding Ephesus as Arsinoeia and keeping a treasure at Pergamon. His rule ended in the son-killing and the battle at Corupedium.
nodes.src: Pausanias 1.9–10; Strabo 13.4.1; Memnon of Heraclea (FGrH 434).

nodes.label: Corupedium
nodes.full: Seleucus defeated and killed Lysimachus in Lydia, the last of the original Diadochi but Ptolemy. He crossed to Thrace to claim Macedonia and was murdered by Ptolemy Keraunos. The disappearance of Lysimachus's kingdom left Anatolia to the Seleucids.
nodes.src: Pausanias 1.10; Appian, Syrian Wars 62–63; Justin 17.1–2.

nodes.label: Seleucus I, Antiochus I
nodes.full: Seleucus I took Lysimachus's Anatolia at Corupedium and was murdered soon after crossing to Europe. His son Antiochus I held the coast and the interior from Sardis, built new cities and fought the Galatians. The kingdom was Hellenistic in its cities and Persian in its structure.
nodes.src: Appian, Syrian Wars 62–63; Memnon, FGrH 434; Welles, Royal Correspondence (1934).

nodes.label: The king’s letters
nodes.full: Seleucid kings wrote letters to the Greek cities, granting them autonomy, exemption from tribute, a gift of grain or oil or the right of sanctuary, in return for honours and loyalty. The cities inscribed them on stone. The Seleucid state ruled Anatolia through such grants and the cities' goodwill.
nodes.src: C. Bradford Welles, Royal Correspondence in the Hellenistic Period (1934); John Ma, Antiochos III and the Cities of Western Asia Minor (1999).

nodes.label: Elephant Victory
nodes.full: Antiochus I faced a Galatian army with sixteen elephants, which, it was said, terrified the Gauls' horses and routed them. Antiochus took the name Soter ('saviour') and the elephant became an emblem of his dynasty. The Galatians were confined to their territory but not subdued.
nodes.src: Lucian, Zeuxis 8–11; Appian, Syrian Wars 65; Memnon, FGrH 434.

nodes.label: War of the Brothers
nodes.full: The young Antiochus Hierax, 'the Hawk', set himself against his brother Seleucus II, took over the Anatolian possessions with Galatian mercenaries and fought on until Attalus I drove him out of the peninsula. It was Pergamon's first great victory over a Seleucid.
nodes.src: Justin 27.2–3; Polyaenus 4.17; Pausanias 1.8.

nodes.label: Achaeus
nodes.full: Achaeus, a cousin of Antiochus III, was appointed governor of Seleucid Anatolia, took the diadem in 220 BC and held Sardis until Antiochus besieged him in the citadel and a Cretan officer led a party up the cliff. Achaeus was killed and the kingdom's Anatolian holdings recovered.

nodes.label: Siege of Sardis
nodes.full: Antiochus III shut up Achaeus in the citadel of Sardis for two years, and took it when a Cretan officer, Lagoras, led a party up the cliff on the side that was left unwatched, the same way that the city had fallen to Cyrus. Achaeus was betrayed and killed.

nodes.label: Ruler cult at Teos
nodes.full: The city of Teos, to thank Antiochus III and his queen Laodice for removing the Attalid and Seleucid armies and for recognising its sanctuary as inviolable, voted them honours like gods: a statue, a precinct, a festival, a priest. It is a model of the way cities used divine honours to bargain with kings.
nodes.src: Teos decrees for Antiochus III (Ma 1999, nos. 17–18).

nodes.label: Queen Laodice
nodes.full: Laodice III, wife and cousin of Antiochus III, received honours from the cities, with a priestess of her cult in the Seleucid kingdom, and was involved in the endowments of Teos. Royal women were the objects of civic gratitude and the channels of petition.
nodes.src: Teos decrees (Ma 1999 nos. 17–18); Sardis inscriptions; Elizabeth Carney on Hellenistic queens.

nodes.label: Philetaerus
nodes.full: Philetaerus, a eunuch officer of Lysimachus from Paphlagonia, held the treasure of 9,000 talents on the citadel of Pergamon and switched to Seleucus in 282 BC. He stayed autonomous for twenty years, and his nephew Eumenes I defeated the Seleucid army at Sardis and made himself dynast.
nodes.src: Strabo 13.4.1–2; Pausanias 1.8.

nodes.label: Treasure of Philetaerus
nodes.full: Lysimachus left 9,000 talents of silver in the citadel of Pergamon in the keeping of Philetaerus, and these became the dynasty's capital. The fund bought the loyalty of cities and mercenaries and financed the buildings of the first Attalids.
nodes.src: Strabo 13.4.1; Hansen, The Attalids of Pergamon (1971).

nodes.label: Attalus I
nodes.full: Attalus I beat the Galatians at the Caicus around 238 BC and took the title of king, pushed the Seleucid pretender Antiochus Hierax out of Anatolia, built the first great monuments of Pergamon and allied the dynasty with Rome against Philip V. He suffered a stroke while addressing an assembly at Thebes in 199 BC and died at Pergamon two years later.
nodes.src: Polybius 18.41, 16.1–9; Livy 29.11; Strabo 13.4.2.

nodes.label: Attalus at the Caicus
nodes.full: Attalus I defeated the Tolistobogii near the sources of the Caicus and refused to pay them tribute, which the Greek cities of Anatolia had done for a generation. He took the title of king and celebrated his victory with monuments that later became famous across the Hellenistic world.
nodes.src: Polybius 18.41; Strabo 13.4.2; Pausanias 1.8.1.

nodes.label: The Dying Gaul
nodes.full: A group of bronzes set up by Attalus I after his Galatian victories showed Gauls wounded and dying, with torcs, moustaches and the wild hair that Greek sculptors gave Celts. The Roman marble copies, the Dying Gaul and the Gaul killing himself and his wife, show the enemy treated with a seriousness the Greek world had not given its foes before.
nodes.src: Capitoline Museums, Rome (Dying Gaul); Museo Nazionale Romano (Ludovisi Gaul); Pliny 34.84; Andrew Stewart, Attalos, Athens and the Akropolis (1993).

nodes.label: Attalus and Rome
nodes.full: Attalus I joined Rome and the Aetolians against Philip V of Macedon in 211 BC and was Rome's friend in the Greek East for the next generation, leading to cooperation against Antiochus. Pergamon was the base of Rome's first campaigns in Asia and the first Asian state with a place in Rome's confidence.

nodes.label: Mother of the Gods
nodes.full: In 205 BC the Sibylline Books and Delphi said that Rome could expel Hannibal if it brought the Great Mother from Phrygia. Attalus I helped Roman envoys to get the sacred black stone from Pessinus, which was taken in a ship to Rome and put in a temple on the Palatine in 191. The Anatolian cult became a Roman state cult.

nodes.label: Eumenes II
nodes.full: Eumenes II fought with Rome against Antiochus III and was rewarded at Apamea with most of the Seleucid lands north of the Taurus. In his reign Pergamon was rebuilt in marble, with the Great Altar, the Library and the Athena sanctuary. He fought Pharnaces of Pontus and the Galatians and was suspected by Rome in the end.
nodes.src: Polybius 21.45–46; Livy 37–38; Strabo 13.4.2.

nodes.label: Great Altar
nodes.full: On a terrace of the acropolis, a great altar of Zeus stood on a podium with a hundred-metre frieze of the battle of the gods and the giants in high relief, a staircase and Ionic colonnade. It is the supreme example of Hellenistic baroque. The German excavator Carl Humann took it to Berlin in 1878–86, where it is the centre of the Pergamon Museum.
nodes.src: Carl Humann et al., Altertümer von Pergamon (1885–); Pergamon Museum, Berlin.

nodes.label: Athena Nikephoros
nodes.full: The Attalids made Athena Nikephoros, 'bringer of victory', the tutelary goddess of the dynasty, with a sanctuary and a library on the acropolis. Eumenes II made her festival, the Nikephoria, a competition with a rank equal to the great Greek festivals in 181 BC.
nodes.src: Pergamon inscriptions (Inschriften von Pergamon, ed. Fränkel); Polybius 22.9; Elizabeth Kosmetatou on Attalid religion.

nodes.label: Library of Pergamon
nodes.full: The Attalids built a library of some two hundred thousand rolls, at the sanctuary of Athena, to rival that of Alexandria. Crates of Mallus, a Stoic grammarian, directed it and made a globe of the earth, and on an embassy to Rome in 168 BC broke his leg and lectured while he recovered. Its rivalry with Alexandria's is said to have produced parchment.
nodes.src: Strabo 13.4.2; Suetonius, De grammaticis 2; Pliny 13.70; Vitruvius 7 pref.

nodes.label: Parchment
nodes.full: Tradition says that Ptolemy forbade the export of papyrus to Pergamon to keep the Attalid library behind Alexandria's, and that Eumenes's craftsmen perfected writing material of prepared skin, charta pergamena. The legend is probably later than the fact, as skins had long been in use, but the name stuck.
nodes.src: Pliny, Natural History 13.70; Varro, quoted by Pliny.

nodes.label: Madradağ pipeline
nodes.full: Pergamon's water came from the Madradağ, three kilometres of pipe in lead and stone, an inverted siphon that ran down 190 metres and up to the acropolis under pressures of some twenty atmospheres. It was the most ambitious pressure pipeline of the ancient world. The Romans later brought water by aqueduct.
nodes.src: Günther Garbrecht, Die Wasserversorgung des antiken Pergamon (1990).

nodes.label: Steep theatre
nodes.full: The theatre of Pergamon, set in the side of the acropolis, has seats for some 10,000 in 80 rows at an angle of 36 degrees and is one of the steepest of the ancient world. The stage was a wooden structure taken down after each festival. The terraced city is among the most dramatic uses of terrain in the Hellenistic world.
nodes.src: Wilhelm Dörpfeld and Pergamon excavation reports (Altertümer von Pergamon, vol. 4).

nodes.label: Arsenals
nodes.full: Behind the acropolis defences of Pergamon, the German excavators found arsenal buildings and stores of artillery projectiles — rounded stone shot of graded weights for torsion catapults — together with mechanisms of winding machines. The kings invested in the science of war.
nodes.src: Altertümer von Pergamon (Arsenals); E. W. Marsden, Greek and Roman Artillery (1969).

nodes.label: Cistophoric coin
nodes.full: After Apamea the Attalids introduced a silver coin, the cistophorus, of lower weight than the Attic standard and valid only in their kingdom, with the basket (cista) of the mysteries of Dionysus on one side and two snakes flanking a bow-case on the other. Cities of Asia minted it, so that the coinage stood for the royal currency area.
nodes.src: Frank Kleiner and Susan Noe, The Early Cistophoric Coinage (1977); Livy 37.46.

nodes.label: Attalus II, III
nodes.full: Eumenes's brother Attalus II, 'Philadelphos', kept the alliance with Rome, founded Attaleia, and in 149 helped to put a claimant on the throne of Bithynia. His nephew Attalus III, a fierce and eccentric man with a taste for poisons and gardening, left his kingdom to Rome in his will.
nodes.src: Polybius 32–33; Justin 36.4; Strabo 13.4.2.

nodes.label: Gifts to Athens
nodes.full: Attalus II built a two-storey stoa at the Athenian agora, with shops on the ground floor, and Eumenes II one on the south slope of the Acropolis. The Attalids saw themselves as the protectors of Hellenism and of Athens, and their gifts made the city a monument to their dynasty. The Stoa of Attalus has been rebuilt as the agora's museum.
nodes.src: Homer Thompson and R. E. Wycherley, The Agora of Athens (1972); Pausanias 1.25.

nodes.label: The king’s will
nodes.full: Attalus III died in 133 BC and left his kingdom to the Roman people in his will, probably to safeguard it from civil war, and Rome accepted. The Gracchi's land bill in Rome used the Pergamene treasure. The province of Asia was the result.
nodes.src: Strabo 13.4.2; Livy, Periochae 58; Plutarch, Tiberius Gracchus 14.

nodes.label: Apollonis
nodes.full: Apollonis, the wife of Attalus I and mother of four kings, was a woman of Cyzicus of modest origins whom Polybius praised for the harmony of her sons. Her sons built a temple to her at Cyzicus with reliefs of famous examples of filial piety, and she was worshipped as a goddess after death.
nodes.src: Polybius 22.20; Anthologia Palatina 3 (the Cyzicus temple reliefs); Hansen 1971.

nodes.label: Magnesia
nodes.full: The army of Antiochus III, with scythed chariots and elephants, was defeated near Magnesia ad Sipylum by a Roman army under Scipio's brother Lucius, with Pergamene troops. Peace was made at Apamea in 188 BC, by which the Seleucids gave up Anatolia north of the Taurus.
nodes.src: Livy 37.37–44; Appian, Syrian Wars 30–36; Polybius 21.17.

nodes.label: Settlement of Apamea
nodes.full: Rome, after Magnesia, made Antiochus III retire behind the Taurus, pay 15,000 talents and surrender his elephants and fleet. The Seleucid lands in Anatolia went mostly to Eumenes II of Pergamon, and Lycia and Caria south of the Maeander to Rhodes, while the cities that had supported Rome were freed.

nodes.label: Rome enters Asia
nodes.full: The war with Antiochus brought a Roman army into Asia for the first time, and the Senate settled Anatolia's affairs by diktat, without annexation. Pergamon, Rhodes and a set of free cities were clients of a power beyond the sea.
nodes.src: Polybius 21; Livy 37–38.

nodes.label: Manlius and Galatians
nodes.full: A Roman consul, Manlius Vulso, marched against the Galatians without senatorial authority, and defeated the Tolistobogii on Mount Olympus and the Tectosages on Mount Magaba in a campaign remembered for its booty. The Gauls were made subject to treaty and ceased to be raiders.
nodes.src: Livy 38.12–27; Polybius 21.33–41.

nodes.label: Chiomara
nodes.full: Chiomara, wife of the Tolistobogian chief Ortiagon, was captured by the Romans in 189 BC. A centurion, who had assaulted her, was killed on her orders when he went to collect his ransom, and she brought his head to her husband. Polybius met her and admired her; the story is a Hellenistic one of a barbarian woman's honour.
nodes.src: Polybius 21.38; Plutarch, Mulierum virtutes 22; Livy 38.24.

nodes.label: Bithynia
nodes.full: The Thracian-speaking Bithynians under Zipoetes took the royal title in 297 BC. Nicomedes I founded Nicomedia in 264, and invited the Galatians across the Bosphorus. Prusias I welcomed the fugitive Hannibal, who is said to have died by poison near Libyssa about 183 BC. The kingdom outlasted all but the Attalids.
nodes.src: Memnon, FGrH 434; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 1–2; Polybius 24; Livy 39.51.

nodes.label: Galatian tribes
nodes.full: Some 20,000 Celts, invited across the Bosphorus by Nicomedes I of Bithynia in 278 BC, settled in the interior in three tribes: Tolistobogii around Pessinus, Tectosages around Ancyra and Trocmi around Tavium. They were mercenaries and raiders, and then a settled people with kings, until the Romans put them in order.
nodes.src: Livy 38.16–26; Strabo 12.5.1–3; Pausanias 10.19–23; Stephen Mitchell, Anatolia (1993), vol. 1.

nodes.label: Galatian tetrarchies
nodes.full: Each of the three Galatian tribes was divided into four districts under a tetrarch with a judge, a military commander and two subordinates, and a council of 300 met at a sacred oak grove called Drynemeton. The twelve tetrarchs and the council made Galatia a federation with Celtic institutions.
nodes.src: Strabo 12.5.1.

nodes.label: Celtic settlement
nodes.full: The Gauls who came over the Bosphorus lived on in the highlands of central Anatolia and kept their own language, so that Jerome in the fourth century AD could say that they spoke the same tongue as the Treveri of the Rhine. Hellenistic Anatolia added a Celtic people.
nodes.src: Jerome, Commentary on Galatians 2.3; Stephen Mitchell, Anatolia (1993).

nodes.label: Galatian mercenaries
nodes.full: The Galatian chiefs rented their young men to kings — to the Seleucids, the Ptolemies of Egypt, Bithynia and Pontus — and Gallic troops fought at Raphia in 217 BC. The tribes lived off their pay and the tribute of the cities.
nodes.src: Polybius 5.53, 5.65, 5.79; Pausanias 1.7.

nodes.label: Pontus
nodes.full: A Persian noble of Cius, Mithridates the Founder, built a mountain kingdom on the southern Black Sea coast after he fled Antigonus in 302 BC. His successors held Amasia and, with Pharnaces I's capture of Sinope in 183 BC, a major Greek port. The dynasty claimed descent from Darius's Seven.
nodes.src: Diodorus 20.111; Plutarch, Demetrius 4; Strabo 12.3.

nodes.label: Pharnaces and Eumenes
nodes.full: Pharnaces I of Pontus took Sinope and invaded Galatia and Cappadocia. Eumenes II of Pergamon, with Cappadocia, Bithynia and Rome behind him, fought him for three years, until Roman envoys settled the quarrel. Pharnaces kept Sinope but had to give back his conquests in Galatia and Paphlagonia.
nodes.src: Polybius 24.1–10; Justin 38.6; Strabo 12.3.11.

nodes.label: Cappadocia
nodes.full: The Persian satrap line of Ariarathes survived Alexander's passing, was driven out and restored in the wars of the Diadochi, and ruled a Greek-speaking, Persian-cultured kingdom around Mazaca, which was a client of the Seleucids until Magnesia and then of Rome. Ariarathes V died fighting Aristonicus in 130 BC.
nodes.src: Diodorus 31.19; Strabo 12.2; Polybius 31–32.

nodes.label: Lycian League
nodes.full: Lycia's cities formed a federation with a council and common coinage, voting by the size of the city, with three votes for the six largest cities, two for medium and one for small ones. Rome gave Lycia independence from Rhodes in 167/168 BC. It is regarded as an early model of federal government.
nodes.src: Strabo 14.3.3; Polybius 22.5, 30.5; Jacques Rouanet et al. on Lycian League studies.

nodes.label: Rhodes at sea
nodes.full: The Rhodian republic, mistress of Caria and Lycia from 188 BC, policed the Aegean against pirates, with a navy and a maritime law that the Romans later admired. After Rome gave Lycia independence in 167, Delos was made a free port and Rhodes's trade declined.
nodes.src: Polybius 30.5; Strabo 14.2.5; Vincent Gabrielsen, The Naval Aristocracy of Hellenistic Rhodes (1997).

nodes.label: Rhodian amphorae
nodes.full: Rhodes and the Carian mainland that it ruled shipped wine and oil in amphorae with stamped handles naming the eponymous priest and the manufacturer. Over a hundred thousand stamped handles have been found from the Black Sea to Egypt, and they date the layers of excavations across the Hellenistic world.
nodes.src: Virginia Grace, Amphoras and the Ancient Wine Trade (1961); Rhodian stamp corpora (Nicolaou, Finkielsztejn).

nodes.label: New temple at Didyma
nodes.full: Seleucus I returned the cult statue of Apollo that Xerxes had carried off, and Miletus began on the site of the burned temple a vast Ionic temple, with an enormous forecourt and a sunken inner court open to the sky. It had 120 columns and was never finished.
nodes.src: Pausanias 8.46.3; Vitruvius 7 pref.; Klaus Tuchelt and Alexander Herda on Didyma.

nodes.label: Artists of Teos
nodes.full: Actors, singers, musicians and poets of Ionia and the Hellespont formed a guild, the Technitai of Dionysus, with its seat at Teos, which had exemptions and a priesthood and sent performers to festivals across the Greek world. Its decrees were inscribed in the city. It was the first professional association of musicians and actors we know of.
nodes.src: Inscriptions of the Technitai of Teos (Sylloge Inscriptionum Graecarum; Sophie Aneziri, Die Vereine der dionysischen Techniten, 2003).

nodes.label: Leukophryena
nodes.full: After an apparition of Artemis Leukophryene, Magnesia on the Maeander sent delegates to all the Greek cities, to the Hellenistic kings and to Rome, asking them to recognise a festival in her honour and the inviolability of the city. Dozens of responses were inscribed on the walls of the agora. The festival put the city on the map.
nodes.src: Inschriften von Magnesia am Maeander (Kern, 1900); Kern's edition of the asylia decrees; Rigsby, Asylia (1996).

nodes.label: The new cities
nodes.full: Kings founded dozens of cities across Anatolia and named them for themselves and their families: Nicomedia, Nicaea, Antioch in Pisidia, Laodicea on the Lycus, Apamea, Attaleia, Philadelphia, Eumeneia. These Greek cities were centres of administration and of Greek language and became the base of the later Roman provinces.
nodes.src: Getzel Cohen, The Hellenistic Settlements in Europe, the Islands, and Asia Minor (1995).

nodes.label: Attalic cloth
nodes.full: Pliny reports that Attalus invented the weaving of gold thread into cloth, and gold-embroidered textiles called attalica were prized in the Roman age. The wool and dye of Anatolia — Sardis, Laodicea and Miletus — fed an industry that supplied luxury to the Mediterranean.
nodes.src: Pliny, Natural History 8.196; Strabo 12.8.16.

nodes.label: Hipparchus
nodes.full: Hipparchus, born in Nicaea in Bithynia, made the best observations of the Greek world from Rhodes and compiled a star catalogue, discovered the precession of the equinoxes and developed a table of chords, the beginning of trigonometry. Ptolemy built on his work three centuries later.
nodes.src: Ptolemy, Almagest 3.1, 7.1–3; Strabo 2.1.

nodes.label: Apollonius of Perga
nodes.full: Apollonius of Perga, in Pamphylia, wrote the Conics in eight books, naming the ellipse, parabola and hyperbola and showing how each arises from the section of a cone. The work is the high point of Greek geometry and was used by Kepler and Newton.
nodes.src: Apollonius of Perga, Conics (Heiberg ed.); Pappus, Collection 7.

nodes.label: Stoics of Anatolia
nodes.full: Cleanthes of Assos in the Troad, second head of the Stoa, wrote the Hymn to Zeus. Chrysippus of Soli in Cilicia, the third, wrote some seven hundred books and gave Stoicism its logic. The school that taught that the cosmos is rational and virtue is enough for happiness was shaped by men from the Anatolian coast.
nodes.src: Diogenes Laertius 7.168–202; Cleanthes, Hymn to Zeus (Stobaeus 1.1.12).

nodes.label: Alexander’s accession and the Persian war
nodes.full: Alexander of Macedon crossed the Hellespont in spring 334 BC to continue his father Philip’s war against the Persian empire.
nodes.src: background — see the Persian Anatolia folio (persian-anatolia-546bc-334bc)
